instructions.task: A persuader is chatting with a persuadee to get them to donate to the charity Save the Children. Tag the final persuader message (after 'Persuader message to tag:') with the persuasion strategy or dialogue act it uses, following the annotation scheme below. Use the earlier chat only as context; judge what the final message itself does.
notes: Pick the single act that best describes the main purpose of the final message.
Anything describing or praising the charity is credibility-appeal; children's suffering is emotion-appeal; arguments that donating is effective or right are logical-appeal.

criteria.greeting: Only a greeting or the how-are-you exchange, with no other content: 'Hi!', 'Hello there', 'How are you today?', 'I'm good, how about you?', 'I am doing well, thank you'. (A greeting attached to other content takes the content's label.)
criteria.thank: Thanks the persuadee or expresses appreciation for their help: 'Thank you', 'Thanks so much for your donation', 'We appreciate any help we can get'
criteria.praise-user: Praises the persuadee or their decision, including a bare 'Great!', 'Awesome!', 'That's amazing!' right after the persuadee agrees to donate: 'That's awesome and generous!', 'You are a kind person'. A 'great!' reacting to other news from the persuadee is acknowledgement.
criteria.acknowledgement: Warm agreement with or reaction to what the persuadee just said: 'That's great to hear', 'I agree 100%', 'This is true', 'Me too', 'I understand', 'Absolutely' or 'Yes they do' agreeing with the persuadee's remark
criteria.filler: A flat filler with no real content: 'Ok...', 'Fine', 'yeah..', 'yes, indeed.', 'Hmm'
criteria.answer-self: A plain yes/no answer or brief reply about the persuader themselves: 'Yes I am', 'No, I'm not sure', 'I'm a student'
criteria.answer-charity: Answers the persuadee's question about the charity, even briefly ('Yes it is!' to 'Is this an American charity?', 'Yes, they are')
criteria.hit-talk: Remarks about the chat task/HIT/MTurk itself or the persuader's own situation: 'we need 10 chats to complete this hit', 'we've chatted 10 times', 'we are poor ourselves on MTurk', small talk statements like 'I live in Florida'
criteria.closing: Ends the conversation or says goodbye: 'Have a nice day', 'I hope you enjoy the rest of your day', 'Bye'
criteria.confirm: Confirms or repeats back the donation the persuadee has decided on, or asks them to confirm it: 'So you will donate $1?', 'Great, so $0.50 it is'
criteria.ask-donation-amount: Asks how much the persuadee would donate, or names a specific amount to ask for: 'How much would you like to give?', 'What amount would you feel comfortable donating?', 'Could you afford fifteen cents?', 'May I suggest $.50 or even $1?'
criteria.proposition-of-donation: Asks or proposes that the persuadee donate, without asking for an amount: 'Would you like to donate to Save the Children?', 'Would you consider donating some of your payment?', 'Donate some money maybe?', 'You can do that right now'
criteria.foot-in-the-door: Stresses that a small amount is enough or is a fine start: 'Every little bit helps', 'Any amount we can collect is welcome', 'Even a few cents makes a difference', 'You don't have to give much'
criteria.self-modeling: The persuader says they themselves will donate or have donated, setting an example: 'I'm going to donate $1 of my payment too', 'I gave what was given to me'
criteria.personal-story: The persuader tells about their own experience: their own past donating, something that happened to them or their family, work they did abroad, what they saw first-hand
criteria.donation-information: Practical information about how the donation in this task works: it is deducted from the task payment, the allowed range ($0 to $2), that the research team will send it to the charity, when or how to pay; also answers to the persuadee's questions about how the donation works ('No, it is not' to 'Is it taken from my bank account?')
criteria.credibility-appeal: Describes or praises the charity itself: what Save the Children is and does, where it works, its history, founder, reach, ratings, reputation, trustworthiness, % of funds to programs, celebrity supporters, its website/URL, that donations are tax deductible, answers to 'what do they do?'; also suffering framed as what the charity is doing about it
criteria.logical-appeal: Reasoning, including moral reasoning, that donating is effective or right: 'Your donation will make a big difference', 'Your donation will be very meaningful to needy children', 'They can only help when people donate', 'Children are the future', 'We should all pitch in', 'Everyone deserves a fighting chance'
criteria.emotion-appeal: Evokes sympathy, sadness, guilt or hope about children: suffering statistics ('1000 children killed in Syria', '5.6 million children die each year'), vivid descriptions of children in hunger or war, stories about a specific helped child or family, 'Imagine how you would feel', 'The children will greatly appreciate it', 'It breaks my heart'
criteria.source-related-inquiry: Asks whether the persuadee knows the charity or what it does, or opens the chat by bringing up the charity: 'Have you heard of Save the Children?', 'Are you familiar with the organization?', 'Do you know what Save the Children does?', 'How do you feel about Save the Children?', 'I'm here to talk to you today about Save The Children.'
criteria.task-related-inquiry: Asks the persuadee's opinion, feelings, interest or expectations about donating, charity or the cause: 'How do you feel about children's charities?', 'Is this something you care about?', 'Have you heard of children separated at the border?', 'Are you interested?', 'Did you know that ... ?'. (Questions about the persuadee's own past donating or volunteering are personal-related-inquiry.)
criteria.personal-related-inquiry: Asks about the persuadee's own life and personal experiences, including their own history of donating or volunteering: 'Do you donate to charities often?', 'Have you ever volunteered?', 'Have you donated before?', 'Do you have kids?', 'Where are you from?'
criteria.off-task: A rare tangent on an unrelated topic, such as a history or politics aside ('the true Americans are the Native Indians'), mentioning a different charity for animals, or 'lovely chatting with you' closing
criteria.misc: Any other message that is none of the above
